tldr: The authors developed GHOST, a teleoperation system that reconstructs a 3D workspace in real time from onboard robot cameras, enabling a single operator to intuitively control two mobile manipulators simultaneously in VR. Compared to a standard tablet interface, it achieves up to 4x the success rate and dramatically improves efficiency in challenging collaborative tasks such as cooperative carrying.
hero_caption: An overview of the GHOST system. Wearing a VR headset, the operator stands alongside the robots like an invisible ghost, intuitively teleoperating two Spot robots within a 3D workspace reconstructed from their onboard cameras.
overview:
Teleoperating remote robots via VR has gained attention as a way to enable intuitive manipulation. However, a single robot has inherent limits when carrying large objects or handling complex collaborative tasks, making multi-robot coordination essential. Previously, when a single person tried to operate multiple robots, they had to either rely heavily on autonomous navigation and provide only high-level goal commands, or juggle multiple screens to perform low-level control individually. This led to serious bottlenecks: operation latency, visual blind spots, and high cognitive load.

To address this, the authors devised GHOST, an open-source VR teleoperation system that relies solely on onboard RGB-D cameras to reconstruct a surrounding 3D point cloud workspace in real time, allowing a single operator to control two mobile manipulators via direct low-level commands. Missing regions in the camera data are instantly filled using deep-learning-based depth completion, creating a unified exocentric 3D workspace around the operator. For control, the system adopts a mode-switching architecture that lets the user smoothly assign and command the two arms and mobile bases using just two VR hand controllers.

In experimental evaluations, the authors conducted user tests with 15 novice participants and 9 challenging collaborative tasks with 3 expert users. The results showed that novices achieved 1.6 to 4x the success rate compared to an off-the-shelf tablet interface. Furthermore, expert trials demonstrated that GHOST enabled the completion of two tasks that were infeasible with the tablet, while running 1.47x faster on average across completed tasks.
contributions: Achieved exocentric VR visual presentation that reconstructs a unified 3D point cloud workspace in real time from onboard cameras alone, significantly reducing blind spots.
Integrated a GPU pipeline with a learning-based depth completion model (PromptDA) to stream high-density 3D point clouds with low latency.
Developed a mode-switching control scheme allowing an operator to intuitively command two mobile bases and arms either independently or synchronously using two VR controllers.
Designed and empirically validated nine dual-robot evaluation tasks requiring bimanual coordination, overcoming blind spots, and spatial reasoning.

sections.heading: Why is it so hard for one person to intuitively operate two robots?
sections.summary: Coordinating multiple robots is essential for complex tasks like transporting large objects, but conventional teleoperation has focused primarily on single robots. When one operator attempts direct, low-level control of two robots, three major challenges arise: cognitive overload, visual blind spots, and communication latency. This work introduces GHOST, an open-source VR system designed to overcome these hurdles.
sections.details:
In complex, unstructured environments, VR-based teleoperation provides operators with spatial depth perception and an intuitive feel for manipulation. However, tasks such as carrying long or heavy items on-site require multiple points of support, necessitating cooperative multi-robot teams. Moreover, a single robot inevitably suffers from blind spots due to narrow camera fields of view and self-occlusions from its own arm, forcing the operator to constantly reposition the robot just to adjust viewpoints.

When one person tries to control multiple robots simultaneously, three main difficulties emerge. First is perceptual integration: mentally synthesizing separate visual streams into a cohesive spatial understanding imposes an enormous cognitive burden. Second is input mapping: seamlessly mapping control channels for two mobile bases, multi-DoF arms, and viewpoint cameras onto two handheld controllers is non-trivial. Third is low-latency synchronized control: streaming and synchronizing multiple video feeds and 3D data over a wireless network in real time is technically demanding.

Previous research has typically either assigned one operator per robot or relied on high-level robot autonomy where the human only provides coarse instructions (such as waypoint navigation). GHOST proposes an entirely different approach: allowing an operator to inhabit the unified 3D virtual workspace as if standing next to the robots like an invisible ghost, directly issuing low-level commands to both mobile manipulators.

sections.heading: Prior approaches in visual feedback, depth completion, and multi-robot control
sections.summary: Visual feedback in teleoperation comes in egocentric (first-person) and exocentric (third-person) forms, with the latter being far better suited for controlling multiple units. Meanwhile, ViT-based depth completion models have emerged to fill missing regions in 3D point clouds. This work unites these advances to carve out a new space enabling simultaneous, low-level multi-robot control.
sections.details:
Visual representations in teleoperation fall into two broad categories: egocentric (showing the robot's own perspective) and exocentric (viewing the robot objectively from the outside). Egocentric displays often induce motion sickness due to discrepancies between camera panning and head motion; with multiple robots, switching between separate first-person screens drastically increases cognitive load. Conversely, while exocentric displays make it easy to understand multiple robots within a single reference frame, conventional setups usually require external motion capture systems or fixed cameras, severely restricting the robots' mobile range.

When reconstructing a 3D workspace in real time from onboard sensors, stereo cameras and RGB-D sensors inevitably suffer from missing depth data on dark surfaces, reflective materials, and distant backgrounds. While NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting yield photorealistic visuals, they remain too computationally intensive for real-time online generation. Therefore, this system focuses on depth completion, using color images as guides to fill in missing depth. Recent trends have shifted from CNNs toward Vision Transformers (ViTs) and diffusion models, but balancing inference speed and generalization is critical for robotics. This work adopts the ViT-based PromptDA model.

Regarding multi-robot control interfaces, prior work has polarized into systems relying on high-level autonomy or multi-operator setups assigning one person per robot. Even among single-operator schemes, most rely on leader-follower formations or coarse trajectory inputs; none offered independent and synchronized low-level control of two mobile bases and arms simultaneously. GHOST fills this unexplored design space.

sections.heading: System Architecture: Fusing a direct GPU rendering pipeline with ROS 2
sections.summary: The physical platform consists of two Boston Dynamics Spot quadrupeds and a Meta Quest 3 headset. To stream high-bandwidth RGB-D data with minimal latency, the authors built SpotObserver, a custom library that bypasses ROS 2 to pipe data directly into GPU memory, rendering it rapidly into the Unity VR workspace.
sections.details:
The hardware setup of GHOST consists of two Spot quadruped robots, each equipped with a back-mounted LiDAR, a 6-DoF arm (with a gripper and gripper camera), and front RGB-D cameras. The operator wears a Meta Quest 3 headset and communicates with the robots over a dedicated Wi-Fi (802.11n) network.

The overall system is structured into three main modules:
- **Unity-based VR client**: Renders the 3D point cloud and robot models for the operator, captures inputs from both hand controllers, and generates motion commands for the robots.
- **ROS 2 server**: Manages lightweight message data such as joint states and robot odometry, handles relative inter-robot alignment, and computes coordinated driving trajectories.
- **SpotObserver (custom library)**: Handles the high-bandwidth RGB-D streams. To avoid message serialization bottlenecks, it ingests data directly from the robot, bypassing ROS 2. By leveraging CUDA and DirectX 12 interoperability (CUDA-DX12 Interop), it performs depth completion entirely within GPU memory, feeding point cloud data directly to the Unity rendering context without extra CPU-GPU memory copies.

Thanks to these thorough optimizations, the system achieves a steady 71 fps headset display rate and real-time responsiveness, even under network bandwidth constraints.

captions.F2: The GHOST system architecture. Lightweight state data and control commands pass through the ROS 2 server, while high-volume RGB-D video is ingested directly by the GPU-optimized SpotObserver library to render point clouds with minimal latency.

sections.heading: Real-time 3D point cloud completion and intuitive visual feedback
sections.summary: Within the operator's field of view, the system presents synchronized URDF models, a real-time merged and completed 3D point cloud, floating gripper camera feeds, and virtual gripper targets indicating goal poses. The PromptDA completion model and LiDAR-based ICP alignment create a high-quality, blind-spot-free workspace.
sections.details:
GHOST provides four key visual elements in the operator's VR space:
- **Real-time robot models**: Synchronized URDF models of both Spots, updated with low latency from joint state data streamed via ROS 2.
- **Unified 3D point cloud**: Point clouds from both robots' front RGB-D cameras, aligned in a shared world coordinate frame and rendered as splats (small disks).
- **2D gripper camera feeds**: Video streams from each robot's gripper camera, rendered as floating sub-displays near the VR controllers. This assists with fine grasping tasks that are occluded from the front cameras.
- **Virtual gripper targets**: Semi-transparent ghost grippers that instantly depict the operator's commanded end-effector poses. Because physical robots lag slightly due to network transit and velocity limits, these ghost targets allow the operator to verify their commanded poses without delay.

In the point cloud pipeline, to correct for individual odometry drift, the system runs an Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm every 4 seconds using the rear LiDAR data, ensuring accurate relative positioning between the two robots. Furthermore, because raw RGB-D data suffers from severe noise and holes, the pipeline applies nearest-neighbor inpainting followed by the ViT-based PromptDA depth completion model running on the GPU via ONNX Runtime. This smoothly reconstructs missing floor surfaces and box contours, yielding a coherent, continuous 3D scene.

captions.F3: Comparison before (top) and after (bottom) applying real-time depth completion. The sparse point cloud riddled with holes is densely completed by PromptDA, dramatically improving the spatial continuity of desks, floors, and cardboard boxes.

sections.heading: A mode-switching mechanism to control two robots with two controllers
sections.summary: To control five subsystems—two bases, two arms, and an exocentric viewpoint camera—using only two hand controllers, the authors decoupled control modes from robot selection. In addition to independent control modes, the system features a Dual-Robot mode that locks both bases into a formation for synchronized carrying.
sections.details:
The Meta Quest 3 provides only two handheld controllers, each equipped with one thumbstick, four buttons, and 6-DoF tracking. The interface must comfortably map five control channels: two mobile bases, two arms, and the virtual viewpoint camera.

To accomplish this, the system decouples robot selection from control modes. In individual operation, the user selects a target robot with each hand and switches between four modes:
- **Fly mode**: Moves the exocentric viewpoint (the operator's virtual position) freely through space using the thumbstick.
- **Drive mode**: Drives and steers the robot's mobile base forward, backward, and sideways.
- **Arm mode**: Directly maps wrist 6-DoF motion to the robot's end-effector. A latching mechanism applies position updates only while holding the trigger, allowing wide reachable workspaces without sweeping arm motions.
- **Arm-Drive mode**: Simultaneously commands base movement and arm repositioning from a single controller.

Even more powerful is the Dual-Robot mode, designed for tasks like carrying large boxes together. When activated, the system records the geometric center between the two robots as a formation pivot. When the operator inputs a movement delta $\Delta T \in SE(2)$ with the thumbstick, the pivot pose updates, and both robots navigate toward their relative waypoints at 10 Hz while maintaining formation. With the bases automatically coordinated, the operator can concentrate on controlling both arms independently in a natural bimanual manner, drastically reducing cognitive load.

sections.heading: Physical experiments: Substantially outperforming tablet control in success rate and efficiency
sections.summary: The authors evaluated the system via a 15-novice user study and an expert study across 9 tasks with 3 developers. Novices achieved up to 4x higher success rates compared to a tablet, while experts completed tasks that were impossible on the tablet and cut task times by 1.47x on average. Ablations confirmed that the 3D point cloud is crucial for task reliability.
sections.details:
The evaluation featured nine collaborative tasks that are challenging or impossible for a single robot: plush toy handover, box carrying, block stacking, trash collection, bag packing, heavy door passage, dustpan sweeping, bedsheet folding, and rope tying. The baseline was Boston Dynamics' official tablet interface, using two tablets with egocentric velocity control.

**Novice User Study (15 participants)**
Participants with little to no prior VR or robotics experience performed the plush toy handover and box carrying tasks. For the handover, GHOST achieved 1.6x the success rate of the tablet, and for box carrying, it reached 4x the tablet's success rate. Completion times for successful runs were comparable or faster. In the System Usability Scale (SUS), GHOST scored an average of 64.8, notably higher than the tablet's 52.8.

**Expert Evaluation (3 experts across 9 tasks)**
Experts compared full GHOST, an 'RGB-only GHOST' ablation (no point cloud, displaying flat RGB panels), and the tablet baseline. On the tablet, dustpan sweeping and bedsheet folding were deemed infeasible by all experts, whereas GHOST succeeded in 26 out of 27 task conditions. Across the seven tasks that the tablet could complete, GHOST was 1.47x faster on average.

**Insights from Ablation**
While RGB-only GHOST achieved completion times close to full GHOST in some tasks, its total success count dropped to 22/27. Failures were frequent in tasks requiring precise spatial alignment and depth perception, such as door passage and bedsheet folding. This clearly highlighted complementary roles: intuitive 6-DoF controller mapping drives task speed, while the reconstructed 3D point cloud provides the spatial certainty needed for high task success.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: Toward imitation learning data collection and autonomy integration
sections.summary: GHOST is the first real-time exocentric VR teleoperation system that enables a single operator to intuitively command two mobile manipulators using only onboard sensors. Future work includes expanding evaluations beyond developer experts, leveraging teleoperation logs for imitation learning (Behavior Cloning), and refining 3D reconstruction quality.
sections.details:
By pairing real-time 3D point cloud reconstruction from onboard cameras with a mode-switching VR interface, GHOST achieves intuitive single-operator teleoperation of two robots. Compared to conventional tablet interfaces, it delivers marked improvements in both task success rates and execution speed.

The paper also openly addresses current limitations. The expert study was conducted by the system developers themselves, which may introduce expertise bias, and novice evaluations were limited to two tasks. Additionally, for thin ropes, deformable cloth, or cluttered scenes, depth completion can produce inaccuracies that occasionally hinder operation.

Looking ahead, the authors highlight several promising directions: using high-quality dual-robot logs gathered with GHOST to train Behavior Cloning models, scaling the framework to teams of three or more robots, and integrating semi-autonomous shared control. GHOST provides a strong foundation for future multi-robot teleoperation and data collection.

takeaways: Running ViT-based depth completion (PromptDA) directly on the GPU enables a practical, exocentric 3D workspace using only onboard RGB-D cameras.
The key to single-operator multi-robot control is the formation pivot lock, which keeps the mobile bases synchronized and frees cognitive bandwidth for bimanual arm manipulation.
Intuitive 6-DoF pose mapping provides operational speed, while the unified 3D point cloud guarantees spatial awareness and high success rates.
Because the system efficiently collects rich, coordinated dual-robot trajectories, it serves as a promising data collection platform for imitation learning and robot foundation models.
limitations: The expert evaluations were conducted solely by the system's three developers, leaving room for potential bias from high familiarity with the interface.
The depth completion model struggles with thin ropes, deformable fabrics, and transparent items; distorted point clouds can occasionally make control harder than using flat RGB feeds.
Point cloud updates are capped at 4.3 fps due to Wi-Fi bandwidth limitations, leaving tracking latency challenges when observing rapidly moving objects.
